Allosaurus.description: A large two-legged hunter with dagger-like, saw-edged teeth, three-fingered hands and small horns above its eyes.[1]
Allosaurus.lore:
Allosaurus was one of the top hunters of North America in the Late Jurassic, tens of millions of years before Tyrannosaurus. It preyed on the plant-eating dinosaurs around it, and Stegosaurus fossils carry its bite marks.[1]

It also fed on the giant long-necked sauropods, though no one knows whether it attacked them alive or ate them after they died. It may even have torn meat from a living giant without killing it, leaving the animal to heal.[1]

Several Allosaurus have been found buried together, and some bear bite marks from their own kind. Whether they hunted in packs is unknown, but they likely competed and fought.[1] No one is sure what the small horns over its eyes were for. They may have helped Allosaurus recognize each other, served as a display for mates, or shaded its eyes from the sun.[1]

sources.title: Allosaurus
sources.publisher: Natural History Museum, London

Ankylosaurus.description: A low, heavy plant-eater covered in bony armor plates, with a beaked mouth and a heavy club of bone at the end of its tail.[1]
Ankylosaurus.lore:
Ankylosaurus was an armored plant-eater from the end of the age of dinosaurs. Bony plates covered its body, and its tail ended in a heavy club.[1] It probably moved slowly most of the time, grazing on ferns, shrubs and fruit near the ground, and it needed about as much food each day as an elephant.[1]

It could not lift its tail club far, but it could swing it hard from side to side, and it probably used it to fend off big predators.[1] It ate only plants, but that does not mean it was gentle: elephants and hippos eat plants too, and both can be dangerous.[1]

No complete skeleton has ever been found, and no one knows exactly how the plates on its back were arranged.[1]

sources.title: Ankylosaurus
sources.publisher: Natural History Museum, London

Ape.description: A large, tailless primate with long arms, strong grasping hands and a heavy jaw.[1][2]
Ape.lore:
Gorillas are the largest of the great apes. A grown male can weigh more than 200 kilograms, stand nearly two meters tall and reach almost two and a half meters from hand to hand.[1] Gorillas spend most of their time on the ground and walk on their knuckles. They are mostly quiet but can scream, bark and roar, and scientists have counted 22 different calls.[1] Older males grow a saddle of silver hair across the back.[1]

Orangutans live high in the forests of Sumatra and Borneo. They are the largest animals that live in trees, with arms much longer than their legs and hands and feet made for grasping, and they are slow and awkward on the ground.[2] They live more alone than other apes. A grown male has big cheek pads and a throat sac that makes his long call boom through the forest for a kilometer or more.[2] Some groups of orangutans make sounds that others don't, habits passed on like local customs.[2]

sources.title: Western lowland gorilla
sources.publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute

sources.title: Orangutan
sources.publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute

Archelon.description: A sea turtle more than four meters long, with large, flat front flippers, a broad, shallow shell and a hooked beak.[1]
Archelon.lore:
Archelon is the largest turtle known to have lived. It swam the warm, shallow seas of the late Cretaceous, about 80 to 74 million years ago, and the biggest one found weighed two to three tonnes.[1] Its shell was more of a frame than solid armor.[1]

It lived in the shallow sea that once cut through the middle of North America, alongside mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, sharks and huge fish.[1] Its hooked beak points to a strong bite. When attacked, it may have struck back with its flippers and beak or used its shell as a shield, though not always with success: bones of turtles like it have been found in the stomachs of mosasaurs.[1]

Like sea turtles today, Archelon probably laid its eggs on beaches.[1]

sources.title: Archelon: The biggest turtle to ever live
sources.author: Hayley Dunning
sources.publisher: Natural History Museum, London

Baboon.description: A large monkey that lives on the ground, with a long tail and olive-gray fur. Males are nearly twice the size of females, with heavy manes and long fangs.[1]
Baboon.lore:
Baboons live in big troops that travel, feed and sleep together. Each evening the troop has to reach a safe place to sleep, up in the trees or on rocks and cliffs.[1] Young males leave the troop they were born in and have to win a place among the males of a new one.[1]

They eat almost anything: fruit, seeds, flowers, roots, insects, eggs and small animals. They can live on grass for long stretches, which lets them survive in dry country.[1]

Baboons say a lot without sound. A hard stare is a threat, made sharper by the differently colored fur around the eyes, and a wide yawn that shows off the fangs is another warning.[1] When a leopard comes near, baboons will mob it, often with the grown males leading the attack.[1]

sources.title: Papio anubis (anubis baboon)
sources.author: Nancy Shefferly
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Badger.description: A low, flat-bodied digger with short, powerful legs and a face striped black and white.[1][2]
Badger.lore:
Badgers are built for digging. The American badger tunnels through soil at speed with its powerful front legs, and it hunts by digging out gophers, ground squirrels, prairie dogs and other burrowing animals. It also eats birds, lizards, insects and even honeycomb.[1] American badgers live alone and come out mostly at night. They don't truly hibernate, but in winter they spend long spells in a deep sleep in their dens, coming out on warm days.[1]

The Eurasian badger is more sociable and lives in family groups, though each badger forages alone. Earthworms are its main food.[2] Badgers growl when threatened and wail when attacked.[2]

Badgers are known for their fierce temper, and apart from people, grown badgers have few enemies.[1][2]

sources.title: Taxidea taxus (American badger)
sources.author: Nancy Shefferly
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

sources.title: Meles meles (Eurasian badger)
sources.author: Annie Wang
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Black Bear.description: A shy forest bear, usually black with a pale muzzle, though some are brown, cinnamon, blond or even creamy white.[1]
Black Bear.lore:
Black bears live in thick woods and rough country across North America. Despite their size they eat mostly plants: grass in spring, berries in summer, and nuts, acorns and fruit in fall, when they put on fat for the winter.[1] Insects make up most of the meat they eat, and they take larger animals only when the chance comes.[1]

They are most active at dawn and dusk, and they spend the winter in dens, coming out in spring thin and hungry.[1] Bears that find people's food or garbage are drawn to it, and that is behind most trouble between black bears and people.[1]

Black bears are clever and curious, with a keen nose and a remarkable sense of direction.[1] They are usually timid around people, and a mother with cubs is far less likely to attack than a grizzly mother.[1]

sources.title: Ursus americanus (American black bear)
sources.author: Tanya Dewey and Christine Kronk
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Boar.description: A wild pig with a thick, coarse coat, often with a ridge of long bristles down its back, and a long snout made for rooting.[1]
Boar.lore:
Wild boars live in groups called sounders, made up of several sows and their young. Grown males mostly live alone and join the groups to mate.[1] They eat mostly plants, such as nuts, fruit, roots and crops, but also eggs, worms, insects, small rodents and carrion, and now and then a lamb or calf.[1]

They forage mostly in the evening and at night. On hot days they lie in the shade and wallow in water and mud, which cools them and keeps insects off.[1] Their sense of smell is keen. They growl when angry and squeal when excited.[1]

Piglets are born with striped coats that hide them in the undergrowth.[1] Boars can do great damage to farmland, and people are their main hunters.[1]

sources.title: Sus scrofa (wild boar)
sources.author: Kristin Wickline
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Brown Bear.description: A huge bear with fur from cream to nearly black. In the Rocky Mountains, white-tipped hairs give it a grizzled look, which is where the grizzly bear gets its name.[1]
Brown Bear.lore:
Brown bears are among the largest meat-eaters on land. Standing on its hind legs, a big one towers about two and a half meters tall, and a brown bear is strong enough to kill a cow with a single blow and fast enough to outrun a horse.[1]

They eat almost anything: grass, roots, berries, nuts, insects and fungi, ground squirrels and marmots dug out of their burrows, and in some places moose, elk, mountain sheep and spawning salmon.[1] In autumn a bear may travel hundreds of kilometers to reach a salmon stream or a good berry crop.[1]

Brown bears usually live alone and avoid people. They rarely attack unless surprised up close, guarding cubs or busy with food, but their temper is hard to predict.[1] Their nose is excellent, able to follow the smell of a rotting carcass for more than three kilometers, though their eyesight is poor.[1]

sources.title: Ursus arctos (brown bear)
sources.author: Tanya Dewey and Liz Ballenger
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Camel.description: A tall desert animal with a long curved neck, a fatty hump, thick lips for eating thorny plants and broad, padded feet for walking on sand.[1]
Camel.lore:
The dromedary, the one-humped camel, is built for the desert. Its hump is a store of fat for hard times, and it shrinks and leans to one side when the camel goes hungry.[1] A double row of eyelashes keeps out blowing sand, and the camel saves water in many ways, including not sweating as the day heats up.[1]

Camels eat thorny plants, dry grass, saltbush and almost anything else that grows in the desert, taking only a few leaves from each plant as they go. They spend long hours grazing and as long again chewing the cud.[1]

They live in small family groups of a male and several females with their young.[1] They are mostly calm, but rutting males fight. When camels quarrel, they shove each other, snap without biting, and sometimes throw up their cud when hurt or excited.[1] People use them to carry loads and for milk, meat, wool and leather, and camels have made it possible to live in some of the driest lands.[1]

sources.title: Camelus dromedarius (dromedary)
sources.author: Robert Naumann
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Cat.description: A small, agile hunter with soft fur, sharp claws, keen ears and long whiskers.[1]
Cat.lore:
Cats probably descend from African wild cats or Asian desert cats, and they live almost wherever people do.[1] There are more than a hundred breeds, but they all share much the same shape and size.[1]

A cat marks its ground by rubbing against things, scratching with its claws and spraying, each of which leaves scent behind.[1] It purrs when content, meows, and growls, hisses or spits when upset. Its ears can swivel to face forward, back or anywhere between.[1]

Cats are meat-eaters, and like all cats they kill with a bite to the back of the neck.[1] Cats gone wild hunt mice and birds, and in some places they have badly reduced the number of wild birds.[1]

sources.title: Felis catus (domestic cat)
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Crocodile.description: A long, armored reptile with powerful jaws that lies almost hidden in the water until it lunges.[1]
Crocodile.lore:
Crocodiles hunt from ambush. The saltwater crocodile, the largest reptile alive, waits in the water with only its nostrils, eyes and part of its back showing, then lunges at prey that comes close. It usually kills with one snap of its jaws and drags its catch under the water.[1]

A young crocodile eats insects, frogs, crabs and small fish. A grown one takes turtles, snakes, birds, wild boar, monkeys and even buffalo.[1] Big males reach six or seven meters long, while females rarely pass three.[1]

The saltwater crocodile is counted among the cleverest reptiles. It communicates with barks, hisses and coughs, and newborns call out as they hatch.[1] A female buries 40 to 60 eggs in a mound of plants and mud.[1] Males guard stretches of river fiercely and drive rivals out to sea.[1]

sources.title: Crocodylus porosus (saltwater crocodile)
sources.author: Erin Wayman
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Deer.description: A slender, quick deer with a reddish summer coat that turns grayer in winter. Its white tail flashes as it bounds away.[1]
Deer.lore:
The white-tailed deer is one of the shyest deer. When startled it bounds off through tangled woods at nearly 50 kilometers an hour, waving its white tail from side to side.[1] It swims well too, and takes to streams and lakes to escape predators or biting insects.[1]

Deer feed mainly around dawn and dusk, on buds, twigs, shrubs and whatever else grows where they live, from maple and birch in eastern forests to cactus in the desert.[1] They keep to small home ranges and wear paths by using the same routes again and again.[1]

They see and hear well but trust their noses most to warn them of danger.[1] They talk with grunts, wheezes and bleats, and a disturbed deer gives a sharp whistle or snort. Glands on their feet and legs leave scent for other deer to read.[1] Wolves, mountain lions, bears, jaguars, coyotes and people all hunt them.[1]

sources.title: Odocoileus virginianus (white-tailed deer)
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Dire Wolf.description: A wolf heavier and more muscular than any wolf alive today, with a big head, powerful jaws and large, strong teeth.[1][2]
Dire Wolf.lore:
Dire wolves hunted across the Americas during the last ice age, from Alaska down into South America, in grasslands, open woods and wetlands alike. Their Latin name means "terrible wolf".[1] They stood about as tall as a gray wolf but were around a quarter heavier, with much larger heads and a stronger bite.[2]

They probably hunted in packs, and thousands of their fossils have been dug from the tar pits of Rancho La Brea in Los Angeles.[1] Horses were their main prey, along with bison, giant ground sloths and camels.[1][2] Many of their teeth are broken, a sign that they fought over carcasses and chewed bone, and when food ran short they may have stolen kills from saber-toothed cats.[1][2]

Despite the name, dire wolves were not close kin to gray wolves. The two lines split millions of years ago and only came to look alike because they lived alike.[1][2] When the great ice age animals died out, dire wolves struggled to compete with gray wolves for smaller prey, and they disappeared about 10,000 years ago.[1][2]

sources.title: Dire Wolf
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service

sources.title: Dire Wolves
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service

Eagle.description: A huge, dark brown bird of prey with long, broad wings and golden feathers on the back of its head and neck.[1]
Eagle.lore:
The golden eagle is the largest bird of prey in North America, with wings more than two meters across.[1] It hunts rabbits, hares, ground squirrels and marmots, and sometimes much larger prey: hoofed animals, coyotes, badgers, and geese and cranes taken in the air.[1] A pair often hunts together, one chasing the prey until it tires while the other swoops in for the kill.[1]

It usually flies at around 50 kilometers an hour but can pass 300 in a dive.[1] Golden eagles are mostly silent. Instead of calling, they defend their territory with a rolling, swooping flight along its edge.[1] Some live in one place all year, while those of the far north fly south for the winter.[1]

sources.title: Aquila chrysaetos (golden eagle)
sources.author: Kari Kirschbaum
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Elephant.description: The largest animal on land, with thick gray skin, great flapping ears, ivory tusks and a long trunk strong enough to lift heavy loads.[1]
Elephant.lore:
Elephants are the largest animals living on land.[1] Their trunk is nose and upper lip joined into one, with no bone in it, and they use it to smell, touch, drink, feed, dust themselves, lift, push and fight.[1] Their tusks are long front teeth of ivory, used to dig for water and roots, strip bark, rescue calves and fight.[1]

Elephants live in herds of related females and their young. Among African elephants a matriarch leads the herd, while Asian herds have no single leader.[1] Young males leave the herd between eight and thirteen years old and spend more and more time alone as they age.[1] They eat leaves, fruit, grass, bark and roots, and they will push over a whole tree to get at its bark or roots.[2]

Elephants call to each other with rumbles too low for people to hear, which other elephants can pick up more than three kilometers away.[1] They are clever and learn much of what they do rather than being born knowing it.[1] Grown elephants have no enemies except people.[1]

sources.title: Asian elephant
sources.publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute

sources.title: Loxodonta africana (African bush elephant)
sources.author: Meghan Howard
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Elk.description: One of the largest deer, with a dark brown mane, a light brown body and a pale rump. Bulls carry wide antlers of solid bone.[1]
Elk.lore:
Elk live in herds that can grow to a few hundred, mostly cows, calves and young bulls. Older bulls keep to themselves or travel in small groups until the fall.[1] Herds move with the seasons, climbing to high meadows in summer and coming down to lower valleys for the winter.[1]

A bull grows new antlers every spring, as fast as two and a half centimeters a day, and drops them every winter. A grown bull's antlers can weigh 18 kilograms.[1]

In autumn, bulls compete for cows. They fight less than they show off, displaying their antlers, necks and bodies and giving off a strong, musky smell.[1] Above all they bugle: a deep call that climbs to a high squeal and ends in grunts, echoing through the autumn nights to warn off rivals.[1] In early summer, cows are fiercely protective of their spotted calves.[1]

sources.title: Elk
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service (Rocky Mountain National Park)

Giant Octopus.description: An octopus grown far past natural size that hides by changing the color and texture of its skin, then seizes prey with eight suckered arms.[1]
Giant Octopus.lore:
The giant octopus spends most of its life alone in a den under a boulder or in a crack in the rock, sometimes staying hidden for weeks. It comes out only to hunt, to mate or to flee.[1] It carries its catch home to eat, and the broken shells of clams and crabs pile up outside the entrance.[1]

It hunts by sight, stalking or chasing its prey or lying in wait, and it can change the color and even the texture of its skin to blend in.[1] Every sucker on its arms can feel and taste what it touches.[1] When attacked, it fights back with its arms, then shoots away and leaves a cloud of ink behind.[1]

It is a clever animal. It finds its way by landmarks, uses objects as tools and learns by watching, and octopuses kept in captivity are known for escaping their tanks.[1] A mother guards her eggs in the den and does not leave them even to eat. She dies before they hatch or soon after.[1]

sources.title: Enteroctopus dofleini (giant Pacific octopus)
sources.author: Colleen Hartis
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Goat.description: A sure-footed herd animal with hollow horns that sweep back or twist like corkscrews. Billy goats grow beards and carry a strong smell.[1]
Goat.lore:
Goats have lived with people for a very long time, and there are many breeds, from small to large.[1] People keep them for milk, cheese, meat, wool and leather, and more people around the world drink goat's milk and eat goat meat than rely on cattle for them.[1]

Goats are social and dislike being alone. Wild herds number from five to twenty, sometimes up to a hundred, and spend the day grazing.[1] Every herd has a pecking order, and the males settle theirs by butting heads.[1]

Coyotes, dogs, mountain lions, foxes, eagles and bobcats all hunt goats. A goat's best defense is its herd, but it will also fight back with its horns.[1]

sources.title: Capra hircus (domestic goat)
sources.author: Adam Mileski
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Hawk.description: A bird of prey with a wingspan over a meter, a brown back, a pale belly and powerful claws.[1]
Hawk.lore:
Red-tailed hawks hunt mostly from a perch, watching for prey and dropping onto it to kill with their powerful claws.[1] Most of what they eat are small rodents, along with rabbits, reptiles and other birds.[1] They also soar over their land on clear days, watching for intruders.[1]

A pair often stays together for years on the same territory and defends it hard. The female guards the nest, while the male drives intruders off the borders.[1] As with many birds of prey, the female is the larger of the two.[1]

Their cry is a harsh, screaming "kee-eeee-arrr", often compared to a steam whistle.[1]

sources.title: Buteo jamaicensis (red-tailed hawk)
sources.author: Tanya Dewey
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Hippopotamus.description: A huge, barrel-shaped animal with thin purple-gray skin, short legs and a wide mouth armed with tusks.[1]
Hippopotamus.lore:
Hippos spend their days in rivers, lakes and swamps, resting in herds of 20 to 100 in water deep enough to cover them, often with their heads on each other's backs.[1] At dusk they come ashore and follow their own worn paths to graze, spending four or five hours a night pulling up grass with lips half a meter wide.[1]

They look clumsy but are not. A hippo can run at 30 kilometers an hour on land, and in shallow water it pushes along the bottom with its short, powerful legs.[1] Its skin oozes an oily red fluid, once thought to be blood mixed with sweat, which works as a sunscreen and keeps germs at bay.[1]

Hippos are loud. Their honking calls carry through the air and the water at the same time, the only mammal calls known to do so.[1] Bulls fight for rank by yawning to show their teeth, roaring, clashing jaws and tusks, and flinging dung with their swinging tails.[1] Apart from people, a grown hippo has no predators.[1]

sources.title: Hippopotamus amphibius (hippopotamus)
sources.author: Kassandra Mason
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Hyena.description: A strongly built, spotted hunter with a massive neck, rounded ears, a back that slopes down from the shoulders and some of the strongest jaws of any mammal.[1]
Hyena.lore:
Hyenas are known as scavengers, but the spotted hyena does most of its own killing. In one study, seven of every ten meals were animals it had hunted itself.[1] It hunts in small groups, or larger ones for zebra, and eats almost anything, from wildebeest and buffalo to ostrich eggs, porcupines and termites.[1]

Spotted hyenas live in clans of up to 80. Females rule: every female outranks every male, daughters stay in the clan for life, and males leave to join other clans, where they must wait their turn for rank.[1]

They are noisy. A whoop calls the clan together, a fast whoop rings out at a kill, and the famous giggle, the hyena's "laugh", comes from a hyena that is scared or excited, often while it is being chased.[1] Lions are their great rivals. The two often steal each other's kills, and their fights can end in death.[1]

sources.title: Crocuta crocuta (spotted hyena)
sources.author: Jason Law
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Jackal.description: A small wild dog with a pointed muzzle, tall pointed ears and a reddish-brown coat.[1]
Jackal.lore:
Jackals live almost anywhere, from open grassland and desert to the edges of towns.[1] They eat what they can get: insects, rodents, hares and small antelope, along with plants and scraps. They hunt alone, in pairs, or in packs when they go after bigger prey, and they wait at a lion's or leopard's kill to pick it over before the vultures finish it.[1]

Their ears and noses are sharp. A jackal on the hunt walks slowly with its ears pricked, and a startled jackal runs off, then circles back in a wide arc to catch the scent of whatever scared it.[1] Jackals are cunning and wary of people, and they turn aggressive only to defend their territory.[1]

sources.title: Canis mesomelas (black-backed jackal)
sources.author: Benjamin Fishman
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Killer Whale.description: A large black-and-white whale with white patches by its eyes. Grown males carry a tall fin on their backs.[1]
Killer Whale.lore:
The killer whale, or orca, is the largest member of the dolphin family and the top predator in the sea. It lives in every ocean, in open water and along coasts.[1]

Orcas live in family groups called pods, built around mothers and their relatives, usually from a few to 20 or more whales, and most stay close to their family all their lives.[1] They talk with clicks, whistles and pulsed calls. Each population has its own calls, which the young learn from their elders, and the calls work like family badges.[1]

What an orca eats depends on what its group has learned to hunt. Off the northwest coast of North America, one kind eats almost nothing but salmon, while another, in the same waters, hunts seals and other sea mammals. They often hunt as a team.[1]

sources.title: Killer Whale
sources.publisher: NOAA Fisheries

Lion.description: A big, tawny cat with powerful forelegs. Adult males wear shaggy manes that range from blond to almost black.[1]
Lion.lore:
Lions are the most social of all cats. They live in prides of related females and their cubs, with one or more males, and a pride can number up to 40.[1] The females do most of the hunting, often closing in on prey from several directions before they charge, and they bring down animals as large as zebra and wildebeest.[1] Lions also steal kills from hyenas and leopards, and sometimes lose their own to groups of hyenas.[1]

Males guard the pride, and both males and females mark their land with scent and with roars that carry for about eight kilometers.[1] Young males are driven out at two to four years old. They band together with brothers and cousins and roam until they can take over a pride, and they usually hold it for about two years before another group drives them out.[1]

Wild lions now live only in Africa, apart from a small population in the Gir Forest of northwest India.[1]

sources.title: Lion
sources.publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute

Mammoth.description: An extinct elephant with long tusks that curve in a spiral, a domed head and a back that slopes down from high shoulders.[1]
Mammoth.lore:
Mammoths were elephants, close relatives of the elephants alive today. Their line began in Africa, and over millions of years mammoths spread across Europe and Asia and crossed a land bridge into North America.[1] Early mammoths ate leaves from shrubs and trees. Later ones grazed the cold, dry grasslands that once stretched across Asia.[1]

The best known is the woolly mammoth, with its thick, dark brown coat. Even woolly mammoths did not live in endless snow. They needed plenty of plants and kept mostly to places where the snow was not deep.[1]

Woolly mammoths were still thriving 20,000 years ago. Over the next 10,000 years they dwindled to small herds on islands off Siberia and Alaska, and about 4,000 years ago the last of them died.[2]

sources.title: Were all mammoths woolly?
sources.author: Emily Osterloff
sources.publisher: Natural History Museum, London

sources.title: The last of the mammoths
sources.publisher: Natural History Museum, London

Owl.description: A big owl with tufts of feathers like horns, a round face, forward-facing eyes and a white patch at the throat.[1]
Owl.lore:
Great horned owls hunt at night and find their way and their prey in the dark, even in thick forest.[1] They watch from a perch, then swoop down, catching prey on the wing if they have to, and they screech loudly as they strike.[1] They eat rabbits, voles and other rodents, and near water they catch fish, frogs, crabs and reptiles.[1]

These owls live alone except when nesting, and they stay in the same area all year.[1] Their deep "hoo-hoo hoooo hoo-hoo" marks their territory and can be heard for kilometers, and fights over territory can be deadly.[1] Some owls have no territory of their own and wander through the lands of others.[1]

sources.title: Bubo virginianus (great horned owl)
sources.author: Drew Dietrich
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Panther.description: A sleek, powerful big cat that hunts by stealth. Depending on where it lives, its coat may be spotted, plain tawny or solid black.[1][2]
Panther.lore:
Panther is a name given to more than one big cat. A black panther is a leopard born with black fur, most often in humid forests.[1] In Florida, the panther is the local puma, a long-tailed cat with plain brown or rusty fur.[2]

The leopard hunts alone, mostly at night. It creeps low until it is a few meters from its prey, then pounces, and if the pounce misses it rarely gives chase.[1] It can take prey up to ten times its own weight, and it often carries the kill up into a tree to eat in peace.[1]

Leopards are at home in trees and climb down head first. They mark their land with scent and claw marks, and they announce themselves with a hoarse, rasping cough repeated again and again.[1]

sources.title: Panthera pardus (leopard)
sources.author: Ashley Hunt
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

sources.title: Florida panther (Puma concolor coryi)
sources.publisher: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service

Plesiosaurus.description: A sea reptile with a long neck, a small head and four wing-shaped flippers that drove it through the water.[1]
Plesiosaurus.lore:
Plesiosaurs were reptiles of the open sea that lived while dinosaurs ruled the land, though they were only distant relatives of the dinosaurs.[1] Plesiosaurus itself was about 3.5 meters long and ate small prey such as fish and crustaceans. Its relatives grew as long as 12 meters, and some had necks longer than their bodies.[1][2]

They swam with four flippers, timing the strokes of the front and back pairs for extra push, and they could not come ashore, so they gave birth to live young at sea.[1] They swallowed stones, which may have helped them break up food or stay steady in the water. Their long necks were stiffer than a swan's and may have helped them sneak up on prey.[1]

Plesiosaurs lasted more than 140 million years and died out with the dinosaurs.[1][2] Mary Anning found the first nearly complete Plesiosaurus skeleton on the south coast of England in 1823, and plesiosaurs later inspired the legend of the Loch Ness Monster.[1]

Polar Bear.description: The great white bear of the Arctic sea ice, with a long neck, a small head, broad forepaws that work as paddles and fur on the soles of its feet.[1]
Polar Bear.lore:
Polar bears are the largest bears alive, and they live on the sea ice around the North Pole more than on land.[1][2] Seals are their main prey, especially ringed seals, and they also take walruses, belugas, seabirds and their eggs, and fish, or feed on dead whales.[1][2] A bear often eats only the fat of a kill and leaves the rest, and younger bears and Arctic foxes live off those leftovers.[1]

Most of a polar bear's time goes to resting or waiting still for prey, and much of the rest to walking and swimming. They are strong swimmers and range far in search of food.[1] Their fur looks white, but each hair is clear, and the skin underneath is black.[1]

Polar bears live alone, except for mothers with cubs. Black and brown bears den up through the winter, but among polar bears only pregnant females spend the winter in dens.[2] A mother will charge a much larger male to protect her cubs.[1]

Pteranodon.description: A large flying reptile with wings of skin stretched from one long finger to its ankles, and a long, toothless beak.[1]
Pteranodon.lore:
Pteranodon was a pterosaur, one of the flying reptiles. Pterosaurs are often called flying dinosaurs, but they were a group of reptiles of their own.[1] Each wing was a thin sheet of skin held up by one hugely long finger and reaching back to the ankle, while the other fingers stayed free as a hand.[1]

Pteranodon had no teeth, yet its fossils have been found with fish in their stomachs. It probably swooped down to the water and snatched fish from the surface, as some seabirds do.[1][2] Large pterosaurs may have flown like albatrosses, riding air currents over long distances and flapping only now and then.[1]

Rat.description: A large, coarse-furred rodent with bald ears and a long, bald tail.[1]
Rat.lore:
Wherever people go, rats follow. The brown rat started out in the forests of Asia and now lives in nearly every port city in the world, in sewers, dumps, basements and fields.[1] It eats almost anything, especially what people throw away, and it also takes chicks, mice, birds and lizards. Rats by the sea have been seen catching fish with their paws.[1]

Rats come out at dusk and at night to dig burrows, forage and build nests. They swim well and learn quickly, remembering their way through tangled sewers and tunnels.[1] Smell is their sharpest sense, and they can feel their way through total darkness with their whiskers and paws.[1]

Few animals have done people more harm. Rat fleas and lice carry plague, typhus and other diseases, and rat-borne disease is thought to have killed more people in the last thousand years than all wars together.[1]

Raven.description: A large, all-black bird with a heavy beak, a wedge-shaped tail and shaggy feathers at its throat.[1]
Raven.lore:
Ravens are the largest of the songbirds and among the cleverest of birds, able to work out new answers to problems they have never met.[1] They are mostly scavengers, drawn to carrion, but they eat almost anything: insects, frogs, small mammals, birds, grain, acorns and fruit.[1]

They are talkers. Scientists have counted between 15 and 33 kinds of calls, from alarms to chase calls to calls that claim territory, and the shaggy throat feathers play a part in how ravens deal with each other.[1] Most ravens live alone or in pairs, but they gather where food is plentiful, and young birds roost together.[1] Ravens soar and glide more than most crows, and their harsh croak gives them away.[1]

Rhinoceros.description: A massive, short-legged beast with thick, wrinkled skin like riveted armor and one or two solid horns on its snout.[1]
Rhinoceros.lore:
There are five kinds of rhinoceros: three in south-central Asia and two in Africa south of the Sahara. They live in grassland, scrub and dense forest, never far from water they can reach each day.[1] Their horns are not bone but solid, packed keratin.[1]

The black rhino of Africa mostly keeps to itself. It feeds in the morning and evening and rests through the heat of the day, rolling in mud to stay cool.[2] It browses on twigs, shrubs and small trees, gripping them with its grasping upper lip, and knocks branches down with its horn to reach higher ones.[2]

Black rhinos see poorly, only 25 to 30 meters, and rely on their noses.[2] A startled black rhino runs off snorting, then often turns back out of curiosity and charges whatever scared it. These charges look dangerous but rarely end badly.[2] Rhinos leave their dung in shared piles, which tells other rhinos who has passed and how recently.[2]

Saber-Toothed Tiger.description: A powerful cat with strong forelegs and two upper fangs up to 28 centimeters long.[1]
Saber-Toothed Tiger.lore:
The saber-toothed tiger, Smilodon, lived in the Americas from about 2.5 million years ago until about 12,000 years ago.[1] It killed with its long fangs, gripping prey with its powerful forelegs and driving the teeth home with a head movement of its own.[1] Saber-toothed hunters may have been able to bring down fully grown large animals, perhaps by striking at the blood vessels of the neck.[1]

Long fangs like these evolved many times, in animals as different as a South American marsupial and the false saber-toothed cats, but Smilodon is the most famous saber-tooth of all.[1]

For all its fangs, its nose was weak. Scans of its skull suggest its sense of smell was poorer than a house cat's or a wolf's, no better than a mouse's.[2]

Swarm of Bats.description: Hundreds of bats that roost together by day in caves, mines and hollow trees, then fill the night air as they hunt by sound.[1][2]
Swarm of Bats.lore:
Bats spend the day out of sight, packed into caves, old mines, hollow trees and cracks in rock, or under bridges, where predators can't reach them. Some of these places fill with bats each spring as mothers gather to raise their young, and others fill each winter as bats crowd in to sleep through the cold.[1] On summer evenings, many come out to hunt insects over ponds and streams.[1]

Bats find their way and their prey in the dark by calling out and listening for the echoes, at a pitch too high for people to hear. When a bat closes in on an insect, its calls speed up into a fast buzz just before it strikes.[2]

Not every bat hunts insects. Some eat fruit or pollen, and a few even catch fish.[3]

Tiger.description: A huge cat with a reddish-orange coat, bold black stripes and a white belly. No two tigers have the same stripes.[1]
Tiger.lore:
Tigers hunt alone, mostly at night. A tiger lies in wait where its stripes hide it, then pounces, drags its prey to the ground and kills it with a bite to the neck.[1] Deer and wild boar are its main prey, but tigers also take monkeys, buffalo, bears, leopards and even crocodiles. They swim well and have been seen hunting in water.[1] A tiger hunts about once a week and can eat as much as 34 kilograms in a night.[1]

Tigers guard their land fiercely. They mark it with scent and claw marks on trees, and they roar, grunt and chuff to keep track of each other.[1] Cubs stay with their mother until they can hunt for themselves and leave at two or three years old to find land of their own.[1]

Tigers once lived across much of Asia, from the lands around the Caspian Sea to eastern Asia. They now hold only a small part of that range, in South and Southeast Asia, China and the Russian Far East.[1]

Triceratops.description: A four-legged plant-eater with three horns, a parrot-like beak and a wide frill of bone behind its head.[1]
Triceratops.lore:
Triceratops had one of the largest skulls of any land animal, with a frill nearly a meter across.[1] It snipped plants with its sharp beak and ground them with rows of teeth at the back of its jaws, and it may have used its horns and frill to push through thick growth.[1]

Its horns were weapons. One fossil horn was bitten off by a Tyrannosaurus and then healed, so at least some Triceratops survived those fights. Males also seem to have fought each other with their horns.[1] In life the horns were covered in keratin, which made them longer and sharper than the fossil bone suggests.[1]

Many horned dinosaurs lived in herds, but Triceratops fossils are usually found alone, so it may have spent much of its life by itself.[1] Its skin was covered in large, pebbled scales.[1]

sources.title: Triceratops
sources.publisher: Natural History Museum, London

Tyrannosaurus Rex.description: A two-legged predator about 12 meters long, with a massive skull, small arms and saw-edged teeth strong enough to crush bone.[1]
Tyrannosaurus Rex.lore:
Tyrannosaurus rex lived at the very end of the age of dinosaurs. Its name means "tyrant lizard king".[1] Its jaws held 60 saw-edged teeth and gave it the strongest bite of any land animal known, strong enough to crush bone. It swallowed the pieces, too: bone turns up in its fossilized dung.[1]

It had a keen nose. Much of its brain was given over to smell, which let it follow living prey or find a carcass from far away.[1] Its tooth marks have been found on the bones of Triceratops and Edmontosaurus, and on the bones of other tyrannosaurs, so they fought each other too.[1]

Its arms were tiny for its size, and no one is sure what they were for. They may have helped it get back up after a fall, or held food while it was young.[1] Fossil skin shows it was covered in scales.[1]

Vulture.description: A big, brownish-black bird with a bare head and neck that feeds on carrion.[1]
Vulture.lore:
Vultures eat the dead. The turkey vulture finds carcasses by smell as well as sight, which makes it one of the few birds in the world that relies heavily on its nose, and black vultures follow it to its finds.[1] It eats roadkill, dead livestock and wild carrion, and it prefers fresh carcasses.[1]

Turkey vultures roost together, sometimes several hundred to a roost, but each searches for food alone by day.[1] They have little in the way of a voice: mostly grunts, hisses and barks to warn off predators.[1] Those in colder lands fly south for the winter.[1]

Weasel.description: A tiny, long, slender hunter with short legs, round ears and dark eyes. In the far north its brown coat turns pure white for winter.[1]
Weasel.lore:
The least weasel is the smallest meat-eater in the world, yet weasels are known for killing prey much bigger than themselves and hiding what they don't eat.[1] It lives almost entirely on mice and voles, and it hunts them by smell, following them into their tunnels underground.[1]

Weasels live alone, and the males are bullies: a dominant male threatens and viciously attacks lesser males, which run off squealing.[1] Weasels bark, hiss, chirp, squeal and trill.[1]

Owls, hawks, eagles and larger weasels all hunt them. A weasel defends itself by blending in or by screeching and biting.[1]

Wolf.description: A lean wild dog with a coat anywhere from gray to brown, black or white, that hunts in family packs able to kill a moose or a bison.[1]
Wolf.lore:
Wolves live and hunt as families. A pack is usually a mated pair and their young, and the parents lead the hunts and teach the young how to hunt, avoid danger and mark the borders of their land.[1] Together they bring down caribou, moose and bison, animals far bigger than any one wolf, and they take rabbits, beavers, fish and even berries when they can.[1]

A pack's land can be huge, and wolves cover long distances across it, mostly at night.[2] They howl to call the pack together, to stir it up before a hunt and to warn other packs away. A wolf cut off from its pack gives a short, rising "lonesome howl", then switches to deeper calls once the others answer, so they can find it.[1]

Around two years of age, a young wolf may wander the edges of its family's land before leaving to find a mate and start a pack of its own.[1] Folklore has long cast wolves as animals to fear, and that fear still shapes how people treat them.[1]
